questions.q: Define politics in one sentence using the terms "collective decision-making" and "resource allocation."
questions.a: Politics is the process through which a community makes collective decisions about the allocation of scarce resources and the distribution of benefits and burdens among its members. A wrong answer that equates politics solely with "what politicians do" or "election campaigns" reveals the student has not moved beyond the common-sense misconception that politics is a separate, dirty sphere rather than a universal social activity.

questions.q: Your school cancels the annual sports day to fund a new library. The student council protests, the principal holds a meeting, and a compromise is reached: sports day returns but scaled down, and the library gets phased funding. Identify the THREE elements in this scenario that make it a political situation.
questions.a: The three elements are: (1) conflicting interests (students vs. administration), (2) scarce resources (budget/time), and (3) an authoritative decision-making process (meeting, compromise, binding outcome). A wrong answer that lists only "protest" or "principal's authority" shows the student sees politics as conflict or power alone, missing the structural necessity of collective choice under scarcity.

questions.q: A housing society has ₹50 lakh surplus. Residents want: (A) a swimming pool, (B) solar panels, (C) a community hall. The Managing Committee can fund only two. Using the concept of politics as resource allocation, explain why this situation is political and propose a fair decision-making procedure the committee could use.
questions.a: It is political because diverse preferences clash over scarce funds, requiring a collective choice that will bind all residents. A fair procedure: (i) publish all three proposals with cost-benefit data, (ii) hold an open deliberation where residents voice needs (e.g., elderly favor hall, youth favor pool), (iii) conduct a ranked-choice vote, (iv) announce results transparently. A wrong answer that suggests "majority vote without discussion" or "committee decides arbitrarily" reveals the student equates politics with raw power rather than legitimate collective decision-making.

questions.q: Compare the politics in a family deciding a vacation destination with politics in a municipal corporation allocating the annual budget. Identify two similarities and two differences in terms of scale, authority, and inclusivity.
questions.a: Similarities: both involve conflicting preferences, scarce resources (money/time), and a binding collective decision. Differences: (1) Scale — family affects 4–6 people, municipality affects lakhs; (2) Authority — family decision is informal/consensual, municipal decision is legally binding with penalties for non-compliance; (3) Inclusivity — family may exclude children's votes, municipality must include all registered voters (universal adult franchise). A wrong answer that says "family isn't politics because no government" shows the student restricts politics to state institutions only.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "If everyone agreed on everything, politics would disappear." Use the concepts of scarcity, diversity of values, and the need for authoritative allocation.
questions.a: The statement is false. Even with value consensus, scarcity of resources (time, money, land) forces choices — e.g., a community may unanimously value health and education but still must decide how to split a limited budget. Politics persists because (a) resources are finite, (b) implementation requires coordination and enforcement, and (c) new issues constantly emerge (e.g., climate change). A wrong answer that agrees with the statement reveals a misunderstanding of politics as only conflict-resolution rather than as the permanent architecture of collective choice under scarcity.

questions.q: Create a 4-panel comic strip or a 100-word scenario showing a non-governmental situation (e.g., cricket team, WhatsApp group, classroom) that qualifies as politics. Label the panels with: "Diverse Interests," "Scarce Resource," "Decision Mechanism," "Binding Outcome."
questions.a: Example: A cricket team (11 players) must choose between batting first or fielding after winning the toss. Diverse interests: batters want to bat, bowlers want to bowl. Scarce resource: the single toss outcome. Decision mechanism: captain consults vice-captain and senior players, then decides. Binding outcome: the team follows the decision. A poor answer that depicts a dictatorship ("coach orders") without showing negotiation or a mechanism misses the collective, procedural nature of politics.
